title: Netflix Just Bought the Entire South. Thirteen Telugu Titans, From Pawan Kalyan to Nani's 'Mad Max', Are Coming to Your Living Room.
excerpt: The streaming giant dropped its 2026 Tollywood slate, and it reads like a who's-who of every megastar you've been waiting for — Ram Charan, Vijay Deverakonda, Fahadh Faasil, even Amitabh Bachchan in a period war epic. The diaspora just won the lottery.
body:
There is a particular ache that comes with being a Telugu film fan abroad. It is the ache of watching a 300-crore spectacle trend on your timeline for a week, the fan edits, the interval-bang screenshots, the uncle in Hyderabad sending you a shaky theatre video at 2 a.m., and knowing you will not see a frame of it for months. By the time it limps onto a streaming platform, the discourse has moved on and you are watching alone, the magic long evaporated.

Netflix just decided to end that ache. The streamer has pulled back the curtain on its Netflix Pandaga 2026 Telugu slate, and it is not a lineup so much as a heist. Thirteen films. Nearly every megastar in the South. And every single one landing on the platform, in Telugu, Tamil, Hindi, Malayalam and Kannada, shortly after its theatrical run. For the diaspora, this is the year the gap finally closes.

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2068680336511242690
"Ram Charan's* Peddi*, directed by Buchi Babu Sana, sold its digital rights to Netflix for a reported 105 to 130 crore, a record for the language."**
https://youtube.com/watch?v=_8J8LwoVH_0
The streamer didn't sign a few films. It signed the whole industry.

Start at the top, because the top is staggering. Ram Charan's Peddi, directed by Buchi Babu Sana, sold its digital rights to Netflix for a reported 105 to 130 crore, a record for the language. Set in 1980s rural Andhra, it has Charan unrecognisable behind a nose ring and a heavy beard, playing a villager who weaponises cricket to defend his community's pride. A.R. Rahman's first single Chikiri Chikiri has already blown past 200 million views. This is the kind of film that, a few years ago, NRIs would have begged a cousin to record off a screen. Now it streams the moment its theatrical legs tire.

Then there is the one that made me sit up. VD14 reunites Vijay Deverakonda with his Taxiwala director Rahul Sankrityan for a period epic set under British colonial rule between 1854 and 1878, rooted in the revolutionary history of Rayalaseema. Deverakonda plays a rugged, meditating hermit, and the director is promising a performance that will shock the audience, but the casting coup is the supporting bench. South African actor Arnold Vosloo, the Imhotep of The Mummy, is reported to play a British officer, and the legendary Amitabh Bachchan is strongly linked to a pivotal role. Bachchan and Deverakonda, sharing a frame, scored by Ajay-Atul. Let that settle.

The slate refuses to stay in one lane. Pawan Kalyan, the Power Star who is now also a Deputy Chief Minister, headlines Ustaad Bhagat Singh, a mass cop spectacle with Sreeleela and Raashii Khanna. Netflix reportedly paid 80 to 100 crore just for the stream. Nani, calling it India's Mad Max, reunites with his Dasara director Srikanth Odela for The Paradise, a brutal 1980s Secunderabad survival saga with Mohan Babu as the antagonist and Anirudh Ravichander supplying the thunder. Netflix grabbed it for 65 crore.

And for those of us who think star power is overrated, the slate has range. Venkatesh finally teams with the Wizard of Words, Trivikram Srinivas, for the grounded family entertainer Adarsha Kutumbam (AK47). Fahadh Faasil anchors Don't Trouble the Trouble, a surreal emotional drama presented by S.S. Rajamouli under Arka Mediaworks. Dulquer Salmaan returns to Telugu with Aakasam Lo Oka Tara, the story of a village girl who dreams of space, tagline: Some journeys to space begin on broken roads. There is a motocross film (Biker), a roommate-from-hell thriller (Production No. 37), a satire on the film industry itself (Vishwak Sen's Funky), and a period football drama (Champion) inspired by the real Bairanpally revolt against the Razakars.

What this slate really signals is a power shift. For years, the streamers treated South Indian cinema as an afterthought, a regional tab buried three clicks deep. The numbers here, the 100-crore-plus cheques written before a single ticket is sold, say something else entirely: Tollywood is now the prize, and the diaspora, those millions of NRIs in New Jersey and Slough and Brampton refreshing BookMyShow for a show that never comes near them, is the audience worth fighting for.

The theatrical purists will grumble, and they are not wrong to. A Nani actioner deserves a packed single-screen, not a paused stream and a delivery doorbell. But for the kid in Edison who has only ever heard their parents describe what a Pawan Kalyan first-day-first-show feels like, this is the next best thing. The whole South, in five languages, a few weeks behind the hall. Pour yourself something. 2026 is going to be loud.
